title: Designing Quantum Solutions to the Closest String Problem with the Non-Variational QWOA
abstract: Quantum computing offers promising approaches to combinatorial optimization problems whose search spaces grow exponentially with problem size. The Closest String problem belongs to this category, which seeks a string that minimizes the maximum Hamming distance to any string in a given collection of reference strings. In this work, we present an end-to-end quantum implementation of the Closest String problem using the Non-Variational Quantum Walk Optimization Algorithm (NV-QWOA), evaluating its resource requirements and solution amplification capabilities. Our automated workflow converts arbitrary problem instances into quantum circuits expressed in one- or two-qubit gates that encode candidate solutions, evaluate the objective function, and apply NV-QWOA optimisation to increase the measurement probabilities of high-quality solutions. Analytical resource estimates yield a qubit complexity of $\mathcal{O}(nm\log k)$ and a circuit depth of $\mathcal{O}(pm\log^2 n + pn\log n)$, where $n$ is the string length, $m$ is the number of reference strings, $k$ is the alphabet size, and $p$ is the number of NV-QWOA iterations. We introduce a revised prescription for the phase-separation parameter, $γ$, that depends on problem size but requires no instance-specific optimization. This prescription mitigates excessive phase wrapping modulo $2π$, which can weaken the relationship between objective values and the phases guiding the optimization dynamics. Across all simulated problem sizes, the algorithm consistently amplifies optimal and near-optimal candidates. This work provides an explicit gate-level implementation, an improved phase-scaling method, and a foundation for hardware experiments and benchmarking against classical algorithms.
summary: This paper presents a quantum algorithm using the Non-Variational Quantum Walk Optimization Algorithm (NV-QWOA) to solve the computationally hard Closest String Problem. The authors provide an explicit, gate-level quantum circuit implementation and demonstrate that the algorithm effectively amplifies optimal solutions in simulations. This work advances the practical application of quantum walks to solve complex combinatorial optimization tasks.
main_problem: The paper addresses the NP-Hard Closest String Problem, which requires finding a string minimizing the maximum Hamming distance to a set of reference strings.
main_result: The proposed quantum algorithm consistently amplifies optimal and near-optimal solutions, achieving high measurement probabilities for the best candidates across simulated problem sizes.
method: They developed an end-to-end quantum implementation using the Non-Variational Quantum Walk Optimization Algorithm (NV-QWOA) within an automated quantum circuit workflow.
model_or_system: The model is a gate-based quantum circuit framework operating on a Hamming graph, utilizing one- or two-qubit gates to encode solutions and evaluate the objective function.
key_observables: The primary observables are the total probability of measuring an optimal solution, the expectation value of the solution cost, and the circuit depth/qubit complexity.
important_parameters: Key parameters include string length ($n$), number of reference strings ($m$), alphabet size ($k$), and the number of NV-QWOA iterations ($p$).
main_assumptions: The work assumes the feasibility of implementing the required reversible quantum gates and provides resource estimates for scaling, while acknowledging the need for larger-scale testing to prove quantum advantage.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the amplification of the optimal state probability over iterations ($p$) and show the convergence of the expected cost towards the minimum optimal cost for increasing string lengths.
paper_structure: The paper outlines the problem formulation, details the automated quantum circuit construction for the objective function, implements the optimization using NV-QWOA, and presents resource estimates and simulation results.
why_interesting: While focused on optimization, the explicit gate-level implementation and the use of quantum walks for optimization provide valuable insights into mapping complex combinatorial problems onto quantum hardware architectures.
